consolidatedFindings.title: Duplicate `rewardTokens` entries pay the same pre-loop snapshot k times and recapture the batch's own donations
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: `_payRewards` transfers `snapshot[i]` once per array element with no cumulative per-token cap, while `_snapshotRewards` writes the same pre-loop balance B into every duplicate slot. The mint loop meanwhile raises the live balance by the batch's own donation D, so k transfers succeed whenever k*B <= B+D.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: The donate-forward mechanic that docs/multi-token-nudge.md §4.2 calls load-bearing is defeated: a batcher recaptures up to 100% of their own batch's donation and can drive the next claimant's seed to zero. Protocol-directed incentive funds (SYA nudgeSplit drip + BalancerPoolerV2 per-mint cut) leak to the batcher that generated them. No user principal at risk.
consolidatedFindings.convergence: THREE independent agents converged: pattern-matcher (PATTERN-001, high confidence, from the ROUNDING-DIRECTION+FEE-ON-TRANSFER duplicate-entry signature), econ-scanner (ECON-002, with mainnet magnitude and the story-016 incident lineage) and story-faithfulness (F-20-01, story-unsafe: §4.5 contradicts §4.2 in the same normative document). Convergence is recorded as CORROBORATION and RAISES confidence to high; it does not reduce the finding.
consolidatedFindings.preservedDetails: ECON-002 carries the most complete quantification (count=400 -> k=9, 704.53 USDC of own donation clawed back; back-to-back steady state nullifies donate-forward permanently) and the mainnet incident lineage (tx 0x6d71d6fd, block 25242986). F-20-01 carries the Law-1/Law-2 framing (the story's own intent is unsafe; §4.5's justification for omitting dedupe is factually false under §4.2's premise) and the independent PoC. PATTERN-001 carries the missing-mitigation checklist. ECON-003 is merged as impact aggregation only — it is explicitly derivative ('no separate code change; fixing ECON-002 restores auction symmetry') and contributes the MEV cost-asymmetry consequence (a duplicating searcher qualifies at ~85% of honest cost and systematically wins the winner-take-all auction) plus the UI-must-populate-an-array-of-zeros amplifier on ledger L-05.
consolidatedFindings.fixTrap: D-16 / F-20-01 rec (c): the obvious remedy — re-read `balanceOf` at payout — is EXACTLY the §4.2 refactor the spec warns against at both the snapshot site and the payout site. A correct fix must clamp to `min(snapshot[i], balanceOf(this) - paidThisPass)` or dedupe, NOT re-read.
consolidatedFindings.witnessGap: DEDUP-20-008 — the §6 witness that is supposed to encode this property runs with D == 0 and passes vacuously.

consolidatedFindings.severitySource: D-22 — settled at Medium on live read-only mainnet evidence, NOT High
consolidatedFindings.title: Step-10 sweep transfers the contract's ENTIRE payment-token balance to `msg.sender` with no `nudgeSize` or `qualifies` gate
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: `uint256 remaining = paymentToken.balanceOf(address(this))` refunds the whole balance rather than the caller's own unspent budget, on any `count == 1` call with empty reward arrays. Whenever a dispatcher returns its own prime token to the batch minter, the pot can leave ONLY through this door — the §4.1 guard simultaneously makes that same asset un-listable as a reward token.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Permissionless, cost-free extraction of an accumulated nudge pot at count=1, bypassing the nudgeSize=40 gate entirely; on a self-sinking wiring the mint is also free.
consolidatedFindings.severityEvidence: D-22 / mainnet-verification-ECON-001.md, read-only Alchemy @ block 25572875: RatchetBatchNFTMinter 0x81896F48… dispatcherIndex()=7, that dispatcher's primeToken()=canonical USDC (mechanic REAL); NudgeRatchet.batchMinter() = 0x86866e01… (REPOINTED — entrypoint==sink identity broken); 0x81896F48… holds 0 USDC / 0 USDS / 0 ETH and archive reads show 0 at the block before the fix, so NO historical loss occurred via this path. Not High (nothing exposed now, nothing ever lost this way); not Low (the sweep at :381-383 is unchanged, 0x81896F48… is deliberately retained and live with USDC as its swept payment token, and one setBatchMinter — or any USDC airdrop — re-arms it instantly).
consolidatedFindings.provenance: D-18: byte-identical since ab07199 [story-013] (2026-05-29). PREDATES story-022 and is unchanged by it. All 22 ledger entries checked — none covers it. Therefore a NEW finding of a PRE-EXISTING defect: not a regression, not a carryover. What is new this cycle is the §4.1 guard, which upgrades the leak from 'dust escapes' to 'the pot can only escape this way'.
consolidatedFindings.preservedDetails: ECON-001 leads (cross-contract path, attack scenario, 3 PoCs, recurrence risk on the Uniboost EYE/SCX/FLX slots, owner-footgun analysis evidenced by the operator's own FixRatchetBatchMinterSink.s.sol). PATTERN-002 merged: same sweep, reached from the pattern DB as eligibility-gate-bypass-via-residual-sweep, proposed potential-high; it contributes the missing-mitigation list and the Law-3 footgun test. F-20-05 merged: proves the same sweep empirically from the spec side and establishes that §4.1's stated threat model ('the thing standing between a caller and the payment-token balance') is prose overstatement — the narrow sub-DUST_THRESHOLD claim does hold.
consolidatedFindings.convergence: pattern-matcher predicted it as a configuration hazard; econ-scanner found it LIVE on mainnet; story-faithfulness proved it from the spec side with an independent PoC. Corroboration.
relatedNotCollapsed: DEDUP-20-003 (the operator-facing guard gap that arms this — separate remedy)
DEDUP-20-004 (the reporting face of the same sweep)
DEDUP-20-005 (a DIFFERENT route to the same pot that the sweep-bound fix does NOT close)

consolidatedFindings.severityNote: Ceiling Medium — escalates if a dispatcher whose primeToken() equals an accumulated reward asset is registered at the pinned index.
consolidatedFindings.title: Nothing ties `dispatcherIndex`'s primeToken to the contract's funding assets, and the removed deploy-time guard was not replaced by an operator-facing one
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: The §4.1 exclusion key and the payment asset are both derived live from `dispatcher.primeToken()`. Repointing the dispatcher — here via `setDispatcherIndex`, or in the SIBLING repo via `NFTMinterV2.replaceDispatcher` — silently reclassifies existing balances. story-022 removed the deploy-time 'nudge token == payment token' assertion and replaced it with a per-call revert that warns the CALLER, never the OPERATOR.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: A routine dispatcher migration performed in a different repo can instantly make an accumulated pot (a) un-listable as a reward and (b) fully sweepable by any count=1 caller. Law-3 non-obvious owner footgun: the coupling is invisible from the yield-claim-nft side. Not owner-malice — in scope.
consolidatedFindings.preservedDetails: CODE-BM20-102 leads (cross-contract trigger, ownerTrustAnalysis, §1 honeypot argument broken). F-20-06 merged: the same root cause from the deploy-script side, naming the concrete collision candidates — PromotionUniV2_Eth has primeToken()==USDC AND donates USDC to batchMinter; NudgeRatchet forwards USDC to batchMinter; only the pinned BalancerPoolerV2 (index 4, primeToken USDS) is safe — and the script's own NatSpec flags DISPATCHER_INDEX=4 as 'ASSUMED… the operator MUST confirm', so a repoint is an EXPECTED operation.
consolidatedFindings.separateRemedy: Distinct from DEDUP-20-002: bounding the sweep fixes the leak; restoring an operator-facing assert (resolve configs(DISPATCHER_INDEX).dispatcher.primeToken() and compare against the intended reward asset, at deploy time and/or in setDispatcherIndex) fixes the signal. Both are needed — kept separate because the mitigations are separate.
consolidatedFindings.ledgerLink: Narrows open ledger L-04 (script/DeployBatchNFTMinter.s.sol hardcoded DISPATCHER_INDEX/USDC nudge token): the USDC half is gone, the DISPATCHER_INDEX half remains and this finding raises its stakes.

consolidatedFindings.title: `totalPaid` floors at 0 on a net-positive call and `NudgePaid` emits the snapshot rather than the delivered amount
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: (a) `totalPaid = paymentAmount > remaining ? paymentAmount - remaining : 0` reports 0 net spend whenever the contract held a pre-existing payment-token balance — i.e. it reads as 'free batch' on exactly the transaction where the caller took someone else's pot. (b) `NudgePaid(recipient, token, amount)` emits `snapshot[i]`, over-reporting delivery on any fee-on-transfer or negatively-rebasing token.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: No direct loss. Any indexer, accounting job or UI keyed on `totalPaid` or `NudgePaid` inherits the error, on precisely the paths where value moved unexpectedly.
consolidatedFindings.preservedDetails: ECON-005. Prong (a) is fixed as a side effect of DEDUP-20-002's sweep bound. Parked MR-BNM-08 covers the same return-value skew from the pattern-matcher side and is carried in manual-review (not merged) per the visible-channel rule.

consolidatedFindings.title: `forceApprove(nftMinter, type(uint256).max)` lets an under-funded batch silently spend the contract's own payment-token balance
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: The approval covers the whole mint loop instead of the caller's actual budget, and the minter pulls from the BATCHER's balance rather than a per-caller ledger. An under-funded batch therefore does NOT revert as documented — the shortfall is covered by whatever payment token the contract already holds (third-party donations, sub-DUST_THRESHOLD dust accumulated across prior batches).
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Directly contradicts the contract NatSpec at :69-71 and §3 steps 5/6. A caller receives `count` NFTs for less than `count` mints' worth of payment and `totalPaid` under-reports the true dispatcher cost. Secondary: the max allowance is contained ONLY by NFTMinterV2's cross-repo property that `_executeMint` pulls from `msg.sender` — an invariant that lives in another repo and is not asserted here.
consolidatedFindings.doNotCollapse: MUST NOT be collapsed into DEDUP-20-002. It is a DISTINCT ROUTE to the same pot with a DISTINCT remedy: bounding the step-10 sweep to the caller's unspent budget does NOT close this route. The two must be fixed together (approve `paymentAmount`, and bound the sweep).

consolidatedFindings.severitySource: D-19 — deliberately held at QA, reasoning recorded so it is not re-litigated next run
consolidatedFindings.title: `minRewards` floors the contract's pre-transfer balance, not the delivered amount; a shrinking token additionally reverts the whole batch
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: The payout amount is a balance snapshot taken before the mint loop and transferred verbatim afterwards. (a) On a fee-on-transfer token the delivered amount is below the declared floor, so `minRewards` does not do what a caller reading it as slippage protection would assume. (b) On a negatively-rebasing or otherwise shrinking token, `safeTransfer(snapshot[i])` reverts and the WHOLE batch — all mints, all other reward tokens — rolls back: a one-token DoS on the entire batch.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Bounded by the tax rate on an asset the protocol does not use, borne by a recipient the caller selected. The token set is permissionless, which is the condition under which the pattern's notVulnerableWhen does not hold — but the caller chooses BOTH the token AND the recipient, the fee accrues to the token's own sink (no extraction), and there is no path by which A's token choice costs an unrelated B.

consolidatedFindings.preservedDetails: PATTERN-005 leads (it carries the extra (b) revert-DoS prong that ECON-006 does not). ECON-006 merged: §4.4 explicitly brings FoT into scope by documenting it, and the binding D-19 adjudication — documenting a risk makes it discussable, it does not manufacture an attack path the value flow does not support. Recommendation is a NatSpec reword only (attribute the shortfall to `recipient`, not 'the caller').
consolidatedFindings.jointFixNote: Clamping the payout to `min(snapshot[i], balanceOf(this))` closes DEDUP-20-001's second-transfer window AND removes this revert-DoS in one change — D-16 directs that the two be evaluated jointly.

consolidatedFindings.title: The mid-loop `onERC1155Received` attacker surface is real and attacker-controlled; the guard holds but NO test in the suite reaches it
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: The inbound acceptance hook fires once per mint INSIDE the loop on a caller-chosen `recipient` — `count` executions of attacker code between the pre-loop snapshot and the post-loop payout, while the contract holds the whole payment budget and a live max allowance. The project's mock minter mints via `MockERC1155.mint()`, a bare balance write that skips `_checkOnERC1155Received` entirely, and the only reentrancy witness proves the guard at the reward-token transfer site with an EMPTY nested reward array.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Not a live vulnerability — the guard is PROVEN sufficient today (D-21: re-entry reverts with the exact ReentrancyGuardReentrantCall selector; a hook-driven mint pulls from the hook, not the batcher). The finding is that §4.3 is certified by a witness that never reaches the hook it was written for, so any future change dropping nonReentrant, moving the snapshot/payout inside the loop, or adding cross-call state re-opens the surface with no test to catch it.
consolidatedFindings.lawRef: Law 1 — an unexercised attacker-controlled callback is a live recall risk, not a cleared row.

consolidatedFindings.title: The §6 witness for §4.5 never configures donations, so it certifies a property that is false in production
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: The witness calls `_fundPots()` only and never calls `nftMinter.setPerMintDonations(...)`, exercising the single configuration (D == 0) in which the §4.5 'fails closed' claim happens to hold. The sibling §4.2 witnesses DO configure donations, so the omission is inconsistent within the same file.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: False assurance for §4.5 — the test passes green while DEDUP-20-001 is live. Re-arm it with a donating dispatcher as part of that fix.
consolidatedFindings.keptSeparateBecause: Different artifact (test vs src), different remedy (re-arm the witness vs cap the payout). Merging it into DEDUP-20-001 would let the coverage regression disappear the moment the code fix lands.

consolidatedFindings.severityDispute: OPEN — requires severity-auditor arbitration. Plausible HIGH for the NFTStakerMigrator orchestrator (user funds permanently lost, no recovery path of any kind). Filed Medium because (a) no attacker is required or benefits, (b) magnitude is bounded by pending accrued on the TARGET pool for users already holding a position there, (c) the solvency invariant is not broken, (d) neither migrator is deployed. Per D-10 the higher reading is recorded, not silently resolved.
consolidatedFindings.title: `NFTStakerDepletion.depositFor` settles a staker's pending phUSD with `_safePay`, paying the MIGRATOR while emitting `Claimed(user, …)`
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: `_safePay` forwards to `_safePayTo(msg.sender, …)`, and `depositFor` is `onlyMigrator`, so msg.sender is ALWAYS an orchestrator contract and never the user. The contract already defines and correctly uses `_safePayTo` in `_exitPosition` (:733) — this is a missed call-site, not a missing primitive. story-021 wrote the fix into the new fourth copy (NFTStakerPriceScaledMigrateReady.sol:887), named the defect in its own commit body ('which would pay the migrator'), called it 'wrong in every case' in the ported NatSpec, and then explicitly left NFTStakerDepletion.sol untouched.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Misdirected user reward plus a false `Claimed` event that misleads indexers and off-chain reconciliation. Recovery is ASYMMETRIC and that drives severity: InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator has an owner `rescueERC20` (recoverable, manual hand-distribution); NFTStakerMigrator has NO rescue function at all, so phUSD routed there is PERMANENTLY STRANDED.

consolidatedFindings.convergence: D-14: THREE independent agents converged — fork-parity (FORK-PARITY-4WAY §3.1 DRIFT-01), story-faithfulness (F-20-03, invariant-violation) and code-scanner (CODE-001, 4/4 PoC). Per the merge rule this convergence is recorded as CORROBORATION and raises confidence; it does not reduce the finding. D-14 also escalates WATCH-17 from a precautionary note to a REALISED defect — the anticipated failure mode (a fix authored in a clone and never back-ported) happened in the very commit that created the fourth clone.
consolidatedFindings.preservedDetails: CODE-001 leads: complete recoverability matrix (grep-verified that NFTStakerMigrator declares exactly two functions, `initiateMigration()` and `migrate(address[])`, with testD probing six plausible rescue selectors, all reverting), the reachability verdict (REACHABLE in realistic migrations via ordinary unprivileged behaviour; NOT reachable on a first-ever migration into a freshly-deployed never-staked target), the solvency analysis (unaffected — committedDebt/rewardBudget decrement identically regardless of recipient), and the safePay call-site audit proving DRIFT-01 is the ONLY instance of the class across all four copies. F-20-03 merged: the story-faithfulness framing — story-021 identifies this exact defect in its own commit message and NatSpec and fixes it only in the new copy.
consolidatedFindings.recommendation: One-line mirror at src/NFTStakerDepletion.sol:756 — `pending = _safePayTo(user, pending);`. Independently add a rescueERC20 to NFTStakerMigrator (DEDUP-20-010) so the class is recoverable rather than terminal.

consolidatedFindings.ledgerStatus: NEW — no existing ledger entry for this root cause.

consolidatedFindings.title: `NFTStakerMigrator` has no rescue function of any kind, no fallback and no receive
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: Its sibling InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator has both `rescueERC20` (:268) and a floor-guarded `rescueERC1155` (:281). Any ERC20 that lands in NFTStakerMigrator — the DEDUP-20-009 misroute, a donation, an airdrop, a fat-fingered transfer — is permanently unrecoverable.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Not an attack. This is the factor that converts DEDUP-20-009 from a recoverable accounting misroute into permanent user-fund loss on the cross-staker path.
consolidatedFindings.doNotCollapse: Distinct from ledgered Q-01 (dead immutable `stakedId` on the same contract) — different root cause, do not collapse. Also kept separate from DEDUP-20-009: different remedy (port rescueERC20) and it stands alone even if the _safePayTo mirror lands.

consolidatedFindings.title: `stake()` is not `poolState`-gated, so any ERC1155 holder can block `finalizeAndReset` and wedge the in-place migration
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: `stake` carries no poolState guard, so a stake during `Migrating` makes `totalStaked > 0` and reverts `finalizeAndReset`'s `require(totalStaked == 0)`. `finalizeAndReset` is the ONLY transition back to Active and `depositFor` requires Active, so this blocks `InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator.migrateIn` for every other parked user for as long as the staking continues.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Migration availability: the in-place rewire cannot complete. Plus a silent per-user yield loss — accRewardPerShare is frozen, so the contract accepts a stake it will never pay on (pendingReward == 0 asserted). Pure-cost griefing with zero attacker profit, and more likely ACCIDENTAL than adversarial since the timeout hatch and the stake button are both legitimate documented user actions.

instances.note: the escape hatch that hands units back mid-Migrating
shrink totalStaked without re-sizing R (price-scaled model only)

consolidatedFindings.convergence: Three agents: code-scanner (CODE-003, 2/2 PoC, verified the pause remedy by EXECUTION not assertion), econ-scanner (ECON-02, cross-contract escalation via claimTimedOut turning 'a griefer could' into 'an ordinary impatient user will', 6-step PoC asserting the re-park re-arms the timeout clock so the loop repeats) and pattern-matcher (PATTERN-003, REWARD-ACCRUAL-ORDER, adding the price-scaled-specific consequence that R depends on totalStaked here).
consolidatedFindings.preservedDetails: CODE-003 leads. ECON-02 contributes the livelock escalation and the silent zero-yield prong. PATTERN-003 contributes the unstake/emergencyWithdraw direction and the observation that the price-scaled variant is materially different from the depletion variant because R depends on totalStaked ('PRICE-SCALED DELTA 6a').
consolidatedFindings.remedy: Add `require(poolState == PoolState.Active)` to `stake`. The sanctioned 'pause first' remedy is GENUINELY COMPLETE (verified by execution: stake/unstake/claim are whenNotPaused while every migration primitive and every user escape is callable while paused) but carries the operational cost filed as DEDUP-20-012.
consolidatedFindings.inheritedDisclosure: D-15 — NOT collapsed into the prior ledger entry. This is the copy-#4 analogue of OPEN ledger L-03 on src/NFTStakerDepletion.sol ('stake/unstake/claim not poolState-gated during Migrating'). A new contract mints a NEW fingerprint that dedup would not link, so the prior entry is NAMED here rather than either silently re-filed as unrelated or silently suppressed as inherited. It is also materially NARROWER on this copy (only `stake` is harmful; unstake and claim settle against the frozen accRewardPerShare and are benign).

consolidatedFindings.title: The 'pause for the migration' remedy halts every registered Phoenix contract; the granular workaround disables the circuit breaker
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: `pause()` is onlyPauser and the registered pauser is the ecosystem-wide Pauser contract, whose `pause()` halts EVERY registered Phoenix contract at once and whose `unpause()` is onlyOwner. Pausing this staker for a multi-slice migration therefore means halting the whole ecosystem for hours or days. Temporarily repointing `pauser` via `setPauser` for granular control disables the global circuit breaker for this staker during exactly the window in which its most sensitive operations run, and breaks the Pauser's register/unregister invariant (`Pauser.register` validates `pausable.pauser() == address(this)`).
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Law-3 footgun: a competent non-malicious owner following the documented 'pause first' runbook step would be surprised it is an ecosystem-wide halt, and the workaround silently removes a safety mechanism.
consolidatedFindings.keptSeparateBecause: Different root cause (pauser architecture) and different remedy (fix DEDUP-20-011 at source so the pause remedy is unnecessary) from the finding whose remedy it costs. The profile asserts the pause remedy is complete WITHOUT costing it; that omission is the finding.

consolidatedFindings.title: `setMigrator` has no lifecycle gate and can be rotated while a migrator holds users' parked ERC1155
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: `depositFor` is `onlyMigrator`, so rotating the pointer immediately bricks the old migrator's `migrateIn`. Parked stake can then leave only via `claimTimedOut`, which returns STAKE ONLY and drops the user out of the pool with no re-accrual and no automatic re-entry. The new migrator cannot reach the parked ERC1155 either — it sits behind the `totalParked` floor enforced by `rescueERC1155`.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Law-3 footgun: the second-order effect (N users' stake stuck in a contract that can no longer return it to the pool) is a step removed from the action (rotating a pointer). Bounded at Low: principal is never lost, `claimTimedOut` always returns stake, and the rotation is fully reversible before any timeout elapses; `migrator = address(0)` mid-migration is likewise non-terminal (permissionless `userMigrate` and `emergencyWithdraw` remain).
consolidatedFindings.remedyCaveat: Gating on `poolState == Active` alone is INSUFFICIENT for the in-place migrator, whose parked custody persists AFTER `finalizeAndReset` returns the pool to Active — the PoC exercises exactly that window.

consolidatedFindings.title: story-021's `_recomputeSchedule()` in `finalizeAndReset` introduces two external calls into the only path back to Active
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: The price-scaled delta adds `nftMinter.configs(dispatcherIndex)` and `dispatcherHook.mintDebt()` to `finalizeAndReset` (NFTStakerDepletion.finalizeAndReset makes none). A reverting hook or minter therefore newly wedges the pool in `Migrating`, which blocks `InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator.migrateIn` because `depositFor` requires Active. The delta itself is CORRECT for the emission model — it closes the depletion copy's ledgered L-02 on this copy — the finding is the new dependency it drags in.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Availability only, non-terminal and unwedgeable (verified by execution): `setDispatcherHook(address(0))` is ungated and performs NO recompute, so it always succeeds and immediately un-wedges; `setNFTMinter` is legal once drained; parked stake exits via `claimTimedOut` regardless; `emergencyWithdraw` bypasses the hook entirely. A widening of the run-19 L-01 in-place-migrator narrative.
consolidatedFindings.trapWarning: Do NOT repoint the migrator at a fresh staker id — that was the run-19 incomplete-fix trap (WATCH-19-L01), it still applies, and it would now also trip DEDUP-20-013.
relatedNotCollapsed: DEDUP-20-015 — a different dependency failure (recipient authorisation) on a different call (`pull()` vs `mintDebt()`), with a different runbook remedy; ECON-08 itself states it 'compounds' this one rather than duplicating it.

consolidatedFindings.title: A staker wired to a `BalancerPoolerMintDebtHook` on which it is not the recipient reverts on EVERY `_syncBudget` path
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: `pull()` is `onlyOwnerOrRecipient` and additionally reverts `RecipientUnset` when `recipient == address(0)`. The staker calls it with `msg.sender == itself`, so stake, unstake, claim, depositFor, initiateMigration and pullAndRefresh all revert unconditionally — even when mintDebt is zero. In a cross-staker migration the target staker is BY CONSTRUCTION not yet the hook's recipient, so wiring its dispatcherHook before flipping `hook.setRecipient` bricks the migration at the first `depositFor`, leaving a partially-executed migration with the batch's ERC1155 already pulled into the migrator.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Availability only — no value at risk; `emergencyWithdraw` and `userMigrate` never call `pull()`, so principal always escapes. Law-3 footgun: the single-recipient hook design is intentional, the undocumented interaction with a two-staker migration is not. The in-repo orchestrator tests never wire a real (or recipient-guarded) hook to the target, so the ordering constraint is untested AND undocumented.
consolidatedFindings.reciprocalHazard: Once the recipient IS flipped, the SOURCE staker's stake/unstake/claim/pullAndRefresh brick too (userMigrate and emergencyWithdraw still work), so the flip must come AFTER initiateMigration.
consolidatedFindings.parkedCorroboration: MR-STK-03 (parked, low confidence) reaches the same un-try/catch'd `pull()` from the DOS-UNBOUNDED-LOOP pattern and is carried in manual-review, not merged — the parked channel stays intact.

consolidatedFindings.title: `unstake` sends the ERC1155 out before the tail `_recomputeScheduleIfActive()`, exposing inflated rate/runway views mid-callback
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: `totalStaked` has already shrunk at :655 while `rewardRate`/`windowEnd` are still sized for the pre-unstake, larger pool when control passes to an arbitrary contract recipient via `onERC1155Received` at :657. `pendingReward` / `currentRewardRate` / `runwaySeconds` read inflated values during that window.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: No in-protocol exploit — nonReentrant blocks every state-mutating re-entry and a grep of src/ finds NO on-chain consumer of these views. Integrator-facing only: a FUTURE protocol pricing against this staker's rate/runway views could be fed an inflated read. That is why this is QA and not Medium.

consolidatedFindings.title: `migrateIn` slice ordering is a value transfer between users: emissions resume for slice 1 while later slices sit parked
consolidatedFindings.rootCause: A migration necessarily drains the pool to zero (`finalizeAndReset` requires `totalStaked == 0`) and then refills it one operator-chosen slice at a time. Emissions resume the instant slice 1 lands, but slice-N users are still in the migrator's custody earning nothing — and because the budget is shared, what slice-1 users collect is drawn from the same `rewardBudget` that funds every later user's runway. Time-in-pool, and therefore payout, is decided entirely by which slice the operator puts a user in: a variable no user controls and none can observe in advance.
consolidatedFindings.impactSummary: Value transfer between users, bounded by targetAPY * (gap between first and last slice) * slice-1 notional; protocol solvency unaffected (asserted in PoC). Measured 1000 bps (Alice 40.685 vs Bob 36.986 phUSD) over identical wall-clock exposure with a 3-day operational lag. At MAX_TARGET_APY (50%) and a 7-day staggered migration the transfer reaches ~0.96% of migrated notional. Law-3 footgun: 'you are not staked, you do not earn' is defensible; what makes it reportable is that the OPERATOR, not the user, chose the un-staked interval, via a migrate-on-behalf primitive.
consolidatedFindings.remedy: Set `targetAPY` to 0 immediately after `finalizeAndReset` and restore it only after the final `migrateIn` slice lands — emissions are then zero for the whole staggered window and slice order carries no economic weight. (ECON-04 measured gas at ~426 users/tx, so single-transaction re-injection is also viable.) Document whichever is chosen as a mandatory runbook step.

refutationsCarriedForward: M-01 depletion rate-drift has NO price-scaled analogue on the ACCRUAL path: R = totalStaked * latestPrice * A / yr is re-derived from live state on every mutation and repeated recomputes are idempotent (budget = V - committedDebt shrinks as accrual commits while the rate is constant), so windowEnd cannot be re-extended for free. The class DOES reappear via the MIGRATION path on the depletion copy — filed as DEDUP-20-018.

Cross-model Depletion -> PriceScaled migration transfers stake value CORRECTLY: batchMigrate returns exact ERC1155 amounts and depositFor credits exactly those amounts with rewardDebt set at the current acc — no retroactive credit, no haircut. The only cross-seam gain/loss is the time-in-pool asymmetry filed as DEDUP-20-017 / DEDUP-20-019; there is no arbitrage in the accounting itself.

NO double-earning across the seam: batchMigrate zeroes the source position and pays the frozen pending before the ERC1155 leaves, and depositFor sets rewardDebt at the target's live acc. The same stake can never accrue on two stakers at once.

story-021's PS-4 delta is CORRECT: NFTStakerPriceScaledMigrateReady.depositFor pays _safePayTo(user, ...) at :887, so the migrator cannot capture a migrating user's phUSD. (The sibling defect at NFTStakerDepletion.sol:756 is DEDUP-20-009.)

Owner-only mid-migration schedule writes (setTargetAPY / topUp / rescueERC20) are economically INERT while Migrating: _updatePool no-ops so nothing accrues at any rate they set, and finalizeAndReset re-derives the whole schedule on the way out.

The mid-loop ERC1155 receive hook is real and attacker-controlled and THE GUARD HOLDS — proven by wiring a hook-firing minter: re-entry reverts with the exact ReentrancyGuardReentrantCall selector (D-21). The finding there is a TEST-COVERAGE GAP (DEDUP-20-007), not a vulnerability.

original.description: `forceApprove(nftMinter, type(uint256).max)` is granted for the whole mint loop instead of the caller's actual budget. Because the minter pulls from the BATCHER's balance (not from a per-caller ledger), an under-funded batch does not revert as documented — the shortfall is silently covered by whatever payment-token balance the contract already holds (third-party donations, dispatcher-side dust accumulated below DUST_THRESHOLD across prior batches). Directly contradicts the contract NatSpec at src/BatchNFTMinter.sol:69-71 ('If `paymentAmount` falls short of the dispatcher's cumulative charge an inner `mint` reverts and the entire batch atomically rolls back') and §3 step 5/6 of docs/multi-token-nudge.md.
original.attackVector: Caller passes paymentAmount = cumulativeCost - X where X <= the contract's own payment-token balance. The loop completes; the caller receives `count` NFTs for less than `count` mints' worth of payment; `totalPaid` under-reports the true dispatcher cost. Distinct route to the same pot as LOCAL-BM20-002 (step-10 sweep) — critically, the profile's recommended fix for BM20-002 (bound the sweep to the caller's unspent budget) does NOT close this route, so the two must be fixed together.
original.secondaryImpact: Cross-repo trust coupling. The max allowance is contained ONLY by NFTMinterV2's property that `_executeMint` pulls from `msg.sender` (lib/mutable/yield-claim-nft/src/NFTMinterV2.sol:183). That invariant lives in a different repo, is not asserted here, and is exactly what an attacker-controlled `onERC1155Received` running mid-loop would need to break to drain the batcher. PoC test 1 confirms the allowance is observably `type(uint256).max` inside attacker code and that today it CANNOT be tapped.
original.recommendation: Approve `paymentAmount` rather than `type(uint256).max`. Functionally identical (paymentAmount is by construction the entire budget the loop may spend), restores the documented fail-closed behaviour on under-funding, and removes the cross-repo dependence on 'the minter only ever pulls from msg.sender'.
original.lawRef: Law 2 (documented behaviour is false) + Law 1 defense-in-depth

original.severityNote: Escalates to Medium if a dispatcher whose primeToken() equals an accumulated reward asset is ever registered at the pinned index.
original.description: The §4.1 exclusion key and the payment asset are both derived live from `dispatcher.primeToken()`. Changing the dispatcher — either by `NFTMinterV2.replaceDispatcher(index, ...)` in the SIBLING repo, or by `setDispatcherIndex` here — silently reclassifies the contract's existing balances. If the new dispatcher's primeToken is an asset the contract has been accumulating as a nudge pot (mainnet today: BalancerPoolerV2 primeToken = USDS, donation = USDC delivered to batchMinter at BalancerPoolerV2.sol:260), the accumulated USDC pot instantly (a) becomes un-listable as a reward — every caller listing it reverts BatchMint__RewardTokenIsPaymentToken — and (b) becomes fully sweepable by ANY `count = 1` caller via the step-10 dust sweep (line 381-387), with no nudgeSize gate.
original.attackVector: Operator repoints the dispatcher (a routine migration action in a different repo with no on-chain coupling to BatchNFTMinter). The next single-mint transaction sweeps the entire accumulated pot for the price of one mint. This re-creates precisely the honeypot condition that §1 of docs/multi-token-nudge.md declares impossible ('there is no configuration of this mechanism under which claiming is profitable-in-isolation') — a pot accumulated over N batches can exceed one mint's price by orders of magnitude.
original.ownerTrustAnalysis: Law 3: this is NOT a malicious-owner vector. A competent, non-malicious operator performing a dispatcher migration would be surprised that it drains the nudge pot to an arbitrary MEV bot at 1/nudgeSize the intended cost, because the coupling is invisible from the yield-claim-nft side. Surprise ⇒ footgun ⇒ in scope.
original.recommendation: Operational: add 'pause BatchNFTMinter and rescueERC20 the pot' as a mandatory pre-step in any dispatcher-repoint runbook. Code: bound the step-10 sweep to the caller's own unspent budget (`paymentAmount - amountSpent`) rather than `balanceOf(address(this))` — this closes the leak for any asset, present or future, and is the same fix LOCAL-BM20-002 needs.
original.lawRef: Law 3 (non-obvious footgun) + Law 2 (§1 honeypot argument broken)

original.description: The inbound ERC1155 acceptance hook `onERC1155Received(recipient)` fires once per mint INSIDE the loop (real path: NFTMinterV2.sol:196 -> OZ ERC1155._mint -> _doSafeTransferAcceptanceCheck), i.e. `count` executions of attacker-chosen code between the pre-loop reward snapshot (line 354) and the post-loop payout (line 378), while the contract holds the caller's whole payment budget and a live max allowance. NO TEST IN THE SUITE EXERCISES THIS SURFACE: the mock minter mints via `MockERC1155.mint()` (test/mocks/MockERC1155.sol:28-32), a bare balance write that skips `_checkOnERC1155Received` entirely. The only reentrancy witness, test_RevertWhen_RewardTokenReentersBatchMint (test/BatchNFTMinterMultiTokenNudge.t.sol:338-354), proves the guard ONLY at the reward-token `transfer` site, and only with an EMPTY nested reward array.
original.verdict: The guard IS sufficient today — proven, not assumed. PoC test 1 wires a hook-firing minter mirroring the OZ acceptance check and confirms: the hook runs NUDGE_SIZE times mid-loop; it observes allowance == type(uint256).max and the full unpaid pot still on the contract; re-entry into batchMint reverts with the exact ReentrancyGuard.ReentrancyGuardReentrantCall selector; and a hook-driven `minter.mint()` pulls from the hook, not from the batcher (batcher payment balance unchanged across the probe).
original.residualRisk: The property is unpinned. Any future change that (a) drops nonReentrant, (b) moves the reward snapshot or payout inside/after the loop, or (c) makes the batcher hold cross-call state, re-opens an attacker-controlled callback surface that no test would catch. §4.3 of the spec is currently certified by a witness that does not reach the hook it was written for.
original.recommendation: Port PoC_BatchMinterCallbackAndAllowance.t.sol's HookingMinter/EvilRecipient into the project suite as the §4.3 receive-hook witness, alongside the existing transfer-site witness. Cheaper alternative: have MockITokenMinterV2 route through MockERC1155.safeTransferFrom (which does fire the hook) instead of the bare mint helper.

dispositions.reason: D-21 REFUTED WITH SOURCE — hostile-token surface is HALF what the Tier-1 profile assumed. This is a PROFILE CORRECTION, not a finding: IERC20.balanceOf is itself declared `view`, so solc emits a STATICCALL at the snapshot call site regardless of the callee's implementation. A hostile reward token CANNOT mutate state, emit events, or mount a mutative re-entry from the snapshot pass — it can only revert (self-harm) or gas-bomb (self-paid). Proven: a non-view balanceOf that writes storage bricks the batch, while the control at count < nudgeSize (where the call site is skipped) succeeds. Reduces the untrusted-token attack surface from two arbitrary-code hooks to ONE (the safeTransfer at :458). Dropped as a finding; the corrected surface model is load-bearing for DEDUP-20-006 and DEDUP-20-007 and is preserved there.

original.description: CORRECTION to the Tier-1 profile. The profile states the snapshot-pass `balanceOf` is 'view-typed but the callee is arbitrary and may mutate state — Solidity's `view` on `_snapshotRewards` constrains *this* contract, not the callee'. That is wrong: `IERC20.balanceOf` is itself declared `view`, so solc emits a STATICCALL at the call site regardless of the callee's implementation. A hostile reward token CANNOT mutate state, emit events, or mount a mutative re-entry from the snapshot pass — it can only revert (self-harm) or gas-bomb (self-paid). Proven by test_SnapshotBalanceOfIsStaticcall (a non-view `balanceOf` that writes storage bricks the batch; the control at count < nudgeSize, where the call site is skipped, succeeds).
original.impact: Reduces the untrusted-reward-token attack surface from two arbitrary-code hooks to ONE (the `safeTransfer` at line 458). Combined with nonReentrant and the fact that the batcher grants no allowance on reward tokens to anybody, every hostile-token vector enumerated (revert-griefing, gas-bomb, inconsistent balanceOf between snapshot and payout, non-standard returns) is self-inflicted by the caller who supplied the array; no third party and no protocol invariant is reachable. Non-standard return values are handled by SafeERC20; a live balance below the snapshot reverts the batch; a token that delivers less than it reports is LOCAL-BM20-003 (FoT), already filed.

dispositions.reason: D-21 REFUTED WITH SOURCE — the `configs` positional-destructure drift is NOT the phStaging YS-20 severity class. Two independent reasons, both PoC-proven: (1) the exclusion key CANNOT desynchronize from the actual payment asset — BatchNFTMinter reads dispatcher.primeToken() (:322) and NFTMinterV2._executeMint reads ITokenDispatcherV2(config.dispatcher).primeToken() (:177) from the SAME dispatcher at the SAME tuple position, so a wrong dispatcher yields a wrong-but-CONSISTENT pair and §4.1 stays enforced against whatever the minter actually pulls; (2) a tuple REORDER displacing `dispatcher` from position 0 FAILS CLOSED — the decoded price-as-address has no code and primeToken() reverts on solc's extcodesize check, bricking batchMint rather than repointing it. An APPENDED field is tolerated, which is the realistic forward-compatible drift. PoCs: test_ConfigsTupleReorder_FailsClosed, test_ConfigsTupleAppend_IsTolerated. Residual (fail-closed is a DoS, not a safe state, and it is emergent rather than asserted) is carried as a QA tripwire in qaHardeningCandidates. The genuinely material drift risk is the SEMANTIC one — a dispatcher legitimately repointed to a different prime asset — which is filed live as DEDUP-20-003.

original.description: The positional destructure `(address dispatcher,,,) = INFTMinterV2(...).configs(idx)` was deferred to interaction analysis against the phStaging YS-20 minter-repoint ABI-drift precedent (filed Medium there). ASSESSMENT: the YS-20 class does NOT apply at YS-20 severity here, for two independent reasons. (1) The exclusion key cannot silently desynchronize from the actual payment asset: BatchNFTMinter reads `dispatcher.primeToken()` (line 322) and NFTMinterV2._executeMint reads `ITokenDispatcherV2(config.dispatcher).primeToken()` (NFTMinterV2.sol:177) from the SAME dispatcher resolved from the SAME tuple position — a wrong-but-live dispatcher yields a wrong-but-CONSISTENT payment token and exclusion key, so §4.1 stays enforced against whatever the minter actually pulls. (2) A tuple REORDER that displaces `dispatcher` from position 0 fails closed: the decoded price-as-address has no code and `primeToken()` reverts on solc's extcodesize check, bricking batchMint rather than repointing it. An APPENDED field is tolerated (position 0 unchanged), which is the realistic forward-compatible drift.
original.residualRisk: Fail-closed is a DoS, not a safe state, and it is emergent rather than asserted. There is no `dispatcherToIndex(dispatcher) == _dispatcherIndex` cross-check (the getter exists on INFTMinterV2) that would turn a silent-decode into an explicit error.
original.recommendation: QA: add `require(INFTMinterV2(nftMinter).dispatcherToIndex(dispatcher) == _dispatcherIndex)` after line 321 as a cheap positional-drift tripwire. The genuinely material drift risk is the SEMANTIC one (dispatcher legitimately repointed to a different prime asset) — filed separately as CODE-BM20-102.

original.severityDispute: Plausible HIGH for the NFTStakerMigrator orchestrator: user funds are permanently lost with no recovery path of any kind. Filed Medium because (a) no attacker is required or benefits, (b) magnitude is bounded by pending accrued on the TARGET pool for the subset of users already holding a position there, (c) solvency invariant is not broken, (d) neither migrator is deployed. Requires severity-auditor arbitration.
original.description: NFTStakerDepletion.depositFor settles an existing staker's pending phUSD with `_safePay(pending)`, which forwards to `_safePayTo(msg.sender, ...)`. depositFor is `onlyMigrator`, so msg.sender is ALWAYS an orchestrator contract, never the user. The user's earned phUSD is transferred to the migrator while `Claimed(user, pending)` is emitted naming the user — the event lies about where the money went. The contract already defines and correctly uses `_safePayTo` in `_exitPosition` (L733); this is a missed call-site, not a missing primitive. The sibling copy NFTStakerPriceScaledMigrateReady.sol:887 uses `_safePayTo(user, pending)` — the fix was written by story-021, explicitly named in its commit message, and not mirrored back.
original.attackVector:
No attacker required. Precondition: the depositFor target already holds a non-zero position with non-zero pending on the TARGET staker. Two proven-reachable orchestrator paths:
(1) NFTStakerMigrator (cross-staker) — the new staker is deployed, wired and LIVE before migration, and `stake` on it is permissionless. Any user who staked directly in the new staker before the operator migrates them across accrues pending there; `migrate([user])` then routes that pending to the migrator. NFTStakerMigrator has NO rescue function → permanently stranded.
(2) InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator (in-place rewire) — after `finalizeAndReset` the pool returns to Active and `stake` is permissionless again; a parked user holding spare ERC1155 units who re-stakes while waiting for their `migrateIn` slice (slices run over hours/days) has their re-accrued pending routed to the migrator. Recoverable there via `rescueERC20` (onlyOwner), requiring manual off-chain hand-distribution.
original.reachabilityVerdict: REACHABLE in realistic migrations for both orchestrators, via ordinary unprivileged user behaviour with no contrivance. NOT reachable on a first-ever migration into a freshly-deployed, never-staked target pool.

recoverability.InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator: RECOVERABLE — rescueERC20(IERC20,address,uint256) at InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator.sol:268, onlyOwner, unconditional ERC20 sweep (parked principal is ERC1155 and structurally out of reach). Owner must hand-distribute. Proven in PoC testC.
recoverability.NFTStakerMigrator: UNRECOVERABLE — grep-verified: NFTStakerMigrator.sol declares exactly two functions, `initiateMigration()` (L70) and `migrate(address[])` (L81). No rescue, sweep, withdraw or recover of any kind, no fallback, no receive. PoC testD probes six plausible rescue selectors; all revert. phUSD is permanently stranded.

original.solvencyImpact: None. `_safePayTo` decrements committedDebt/rewardBudget identically regardless of recipient, so `balance == rewardBudget + committedDebt` is preserved. The loss is entirely to the individual user.

original.description: `stake()` carries no poolState guard. Any ERC1155 holder can stake while poolState == Migrating, making totalStaked > 0 and reverting finalizeAndReset's `require(totalStaked == 0)`. finalizeAndReset is the ONLY transition back to Active and depositFor requires Active, so this blocks InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator.migrateIn for as long as the griefer keeps re-staking. Copy-#4 analogue of the OPEN ledgered L-03 on src/NFTStakerDepletion.sol, but narrower: only `stake` is harmful here — `unstake` and `claim` during Migrating settle against the frozen accRewardPerShare and are benign (unstake actively helps the drain).
original.attackVector: Griefer buys/holds 1 ERC1155 unit and front-runs each finalizeAndReset with a stake. Operator evicts via migrateOut (which parks the unit and re-zeroes totalStaked) but the two calls live on different contracts and cannot be atomically batched by an EOA owner, so the griefer can wedge between them each round. Cost is gas plus capital lockup of one unit per round (returned via claimTimedOut after >= 1 day); no principal is burned. The griefer earns nothing — accRewardPerShare is frozen, so a Migrating-window stake accrues zero. Pure-cost griefing, cheap per round.
original.remedyVerdict: The profile's 'pause first' remedy is GENUINELY COMPLETE and was verified by execution, not accepted: stake/unstake/claim are whenNotPaused (L617/645/666) while initiateMigration (L774), batchMigrate (L797), depositFor (L879), finalizeAndReset (L925), emergencyWithdraw (L735) and userMigrate (L827) all carry no whenNotPaused. A full pause -> initiateMigration -> migrateOut -> finalizeAndReset -> migrateIn cycle completes while paused with the user fully round-tripped, and stake reverts throughout. See CODE-004 for the operational cost of that remedy.
original.recommendation: Add `require(poolState == PoolState.Active, "NFTStaker: not active")` to `stake`. This is strictly better than the pause remedy: it is granular, costs the ecosystem nothing, and removes the dependency on operator discipline. Owner-batching migrateOut+finalizeAndReset via a Safe multicall is a partial mitigation only.

original.description: CODE-003's sanctioned remedy is 'pause for the duration of the migration', but `pause()` is onlyPauser and the registered pauser is the ecosystem-wide Pauser contract (lib/mutable/pauser/src/Pauser.sol), whose `pause()` halts EVERY registered Phoenix contract at once and whose `unpause()` is onlyOwner. Pausing this staker for a multi-slice migration therefore means halting the whole ecosystem for hours or days. The alternative — temporarily repointing `pauser` via setPauser to an operator address for granular control — disables the global circuit breaker for this staker during exactly the window in which its most sensitive operations run, and also breaks the Pauser's register/unregister invariant (Pauser.register validates `pausable.pauser() == address(this)`).
original.attackVector: None. This is a Law-3 footgun: a competent non-malicious owner following the documented 'pause first' runbook step would be surprised to learn it is an ecosystem-wide halt, and the granular workaround silently removes a safety mechanism.

original.description: setMigrator has no lifecycle gate — it is callable while poolState == Migrating and while an InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator holds users' parked ERC1155. Because depositFor is onlyMigrator, rotating the pointer immediately bricks the old migrator's migrateIn: parked stake can then leave only via claimTimedOut, which returns STAKE ONLY and drops the user out of the pool with no re-accrual and no automatic re-entry. The new migrator cannot reach the parked ERC1155 either — it sits in the old migrator behind the totalParked floor enforced by rescueERC1155 (L281-289).
original.attackVector: No attacker. Law-3 footgun test: the second-order effect (N users' stake is now stuck in a contract that can no longer return it to the pool) is a step removed from the action (rotating a pointer). A competent, non-malicious owner WOULD be surprised — in scope.
original.boundedness: Principal is never lost: claimTimedOut always returns stake to its owner, and the rotation is fully reversible by pointing `migrator` back before any timeout elapses. Setting migrator to address(0) mid-migration is likewise non-terminal — users self-exit via the permissionless userMigrate (Migrating-only) or emergencyWithdraw. This bounds the finding at Low.
original.recommendation: Gate setMigrator on `poolState == PoolState.Active`, or document the rotation hazard in the migration runbook. Note the Active gate alone is insufficient for the in-place migrator, whose parked custody persists after finalizeAndReset returns the pool to Active — the PoC exercises exactly that window.

original.description: The story-021 price-scaled delta adds `_recomputeSchedule()` to finalizeAndReset — correct for the emission model (it closes the depletion copy's ledgered L-02 on this copy), but it introduces two external calls into the revival path: `nftMinter.configs(dispatcherIndex)` and `dispatcherHook.mintDebt()`. NFTStakerDepletion.finalizeAndReset makes none. A reverting hook or minter therefore newly wedges the pool in Migrating, which in turn blocks InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator.migrateIn (depositFor requires Active). This is a widening of the run-19 L-01 in-place-migrator narrative.
original.attackVector: No attacker; a dependency failure. The dispatcherHook is owner-settable and live-rotatable, so a bad rotation or an upstream yield-claim-nft incident is the realistic trigger.
original.boundedness: Non-terminal and unwedgeable. Verified by execution: setDispatcherHook(address(0)) is ungated and performs NO recompute (L356-359), so it always succeeds and immediately un-wedges finalizeAndReset. setNFTMinter is legal once drained (totalStaked == 0 is already a finalizeAndReset precondition). Parked stake exits via claimTimedOut regardless, the totalParked floor holds, and emergencyWithdraw bypasses the hook entirely (proven).
original.recommendation: Runbook only: if either dependency is unhealthy, run setDispatcherHook(0) and/or setNFTMinter(good) BEFORE finalizeAndReset. Do NOT repoint the migrator at a fresh staker id — that was the run-19 incomplete-fix trap and it still applies (and would now also trip CODE-005).

original.description: unstake sends the ERC1155 out to msg.sender at L657, handing an arbitrary contract recipient control via onERC1155Received, and only then runs the tail `_recomputeScheduleIfActive()` at L663. During that callback window totalStaked has already shrunk (L655) while rewardRate/windowEnd are still sized for the pre-unstake, larger pool, so pendingReward / currentRewardRate / runwaySeconds read inflated values.
original.attackVector: No in-protocol exploit — nonReentrant blocks every state-mutating re-entry, and a grep of src/ finds NO on-chain consumer of these views. The exposure is integrator-facing only: a future protocol that prices against this staker's rate/runway views could be fed an inflated read mid-callback. That is why this is QA and not Medium.
original.recommendation: Move `_recomputeScheduleIfActive()` above the L657 transfer — nothing between them depends on the transfer, so the change is free and behaviour-preserving, and it restores strict CEI. Note stake, claim, emergencyWithdraw, batchMigrate, userMigrate and _exitPosition are all already clean (position zeroed and debt settled before any outbound send, no post-transfer writes), so this is a single isolated call-site, not a pattern.

original.type: cross-contract value leak / unbounded balance sweep
original.severityNote: Re-rate HIGH if `cast call 0x7A4eD11160A06bB1C5b59091575d59707BE97a72 'batchMinter()(address)' --rpc-url $RPC_MAINNET` still returns 0x81896f48a95abea255cd38a3010e985b6051a1c7. In that state the drain is permissionless, free, and unmitigated (no pauser is set on 0x81896…). If it returns 0x86866e01a115C17892Ed04c548F2e8638851029d the corrective script has been broadcast and the live instance is safe — but the CODE-LEVEL defect below is unfixed either way.
original.description: Step 10 sweeps the contract's ENTIRE payment-token balance to msg.sender — not the caller's unspent budget — and is gated by neither `nudgeSize` nor `qualifies`. Whenever a dispatcher returns its own prime token to the batch minter, this converts the nudge pot into a permissionless, cost-free withdrawal at count=1, while the §4.1 guard (L426-428) simultaneously makes that same asset un-listable as a `rewardTokens` entry — so the pot can ONLY leave through the wrong door. The profiler recorded this as hypothetical (trust assumption #3, 'if a future dispatcher ever donated its own prime token'). It is not hypothetical: NudgeRatchet does exactly this by design and was deployed that way on mainnet.
original.crossContractPath: NudgeRatchet.sol:104 `IERC20(_token).safeTransfer(batchMinter, bal)` forwards 100% of the USDC mint price to `batchMinter`. DeployMainnetNudgeRatchet.s.sol:342 sets `batchMinter_ = ratchetBatchNFTMinter`; :458 sets `RatchetBatchNFTMinter.setDispatcherIndex(7)`. Therefore paymentToken == NudgeRatchet.primeToken() == USDC == the donated asset. Entrypoint and sink are the same contract.
original.attackScenario:
1. Honest users mint ratchet NFTs at 10 USDC each through the UI; every mint parks 10 USDC on RatchetBatchNFTMinter as the intended nudge bounty.
2. Attacker calls batchMint(count=1, recipient=self, paymentAmount=10 USDC, [], []). No qualification, no reward array.
3. The single mint's 10 USDC round-trips back into the contract via the ratchet.
4. Step 10 reads balanceOf(this) — the whole accumulated pot plus the attacker's own payment — and transfers all of it to msg.sender.
5. Attacker keeps the pot, keeps their payment (the mint was free), and keeps the NFT.
original.economicImpact: 100% of ratchet mint revenue is extractable by any address for gas only. The nudgeSize=40 gate is fully bypassed. Also makes every batchMint through this instance a free mint, so the ERC1155 units — and the 45%-APY phUSD staking stream they unlock on NFTStakerPriceScaled — are acquired at zero net cost while the mint-debt hook has already accrued phUSD against them.
original.profitability: Unconditionally profitable: the extraction cost is one mint whose payment is refunded in the same transaction. Gas only. Repeatable every time the pot refills.
affectedParties: honest ratchet minters whose contribution funds the bounty
the intended 40-batcher who can never win it
poc: PoC_RatchetPrimeTokenSweep.test_RatchetBatchMintIsFree — caller's USDC balance unchanged after 5 mints, receives all 5 NFTs, totalPaid == 0
PoC_RatchetPrimeTokenSweep.test_CountOneCallerSweepsEntireRatchetPot — 2,000 USDC pot from 200 honest direct mints drained by a count=1 caller who also keeps their payment
PoC_RatchetPrimeTokenSweep.test_QualifyingBatcherCannotListThePotAsset — the legitimate 40-batcher reverts BatchMint__RewardTokenIsPaymentToken on the very asset the count=1 caller walked off with
original.ownerFootgunAnalysis: Law 3 in-scope. A competent, non-malicious owner made exactly this wiring choice on mainnet and was surprised by it — the corrective script FixRatchetBatchMinterSink.s.sol:12-22 documents the discovery in the operator's own words ('a ratchet batchMint swept its own USDC back in during the loop and then refunded it to the caller'). It was caught by a single smoke-test mint, not by any contract-level signal. The contract offers no guard, no revert, and no event distinguishing 'refund of my surplus' from 'sweep of someone else's pot'.
original.recurrenceRisk: The fix is operational (repoint the sink), not structural, and the same class is one setter away on the Uniboost path: Uniboost._dispatch donates `donationSplit`% of the PRIME token to `recipient` (currently 50%, pointed at 0x86866e whose payment token is USDS, so safe today). mainnet-addresses.ts:99-105 reserves EyeBatchNFTMinter / ScxBatchNFTMinter / FlxBatchNFTMinter slots. If any of those is deployed as the UI entrypoint for its Uniboost dispatcher and `Uniboost.setRecipient` is pointed at it — the natural symmetric choice, and precisely what was done for the ratchet — 50% of every EYE/SCX/FLX mint becomes a free count=1 sweep.
original.recommendation: Bound the sweep to the caller's own unspent budget instead of reading balanceOf. Track spend explicitly (record paymentToken.balanceOf(address(this)) BEFORE the step-5 pull as `preExisting`, then refund `min(remaining, remaining - preExisting)`), or gate the sweep to `remaining - preExisting`. This also fixes the totalPaid mis-report (ECON-005). Cheaper defensive alternative: revert in batchMint if the post-loop payment-token balance exceeds the pre-pull balance plus paymentAmount, which fails closed on any self-sink wiring. Correct §4.1 and the contract NatSpec at L51-L56, which currently imply the payment token is protected when it is in fact the least protected asset the contract holds.
original.provenance: The sweep is byte-identical since ab07199 [story-013] (2026-05-29) — it PREDATES story-022 and is unchanged by it. There is NO existing ledger entry for it (checked reports/phoenix-nft-staking/ledger.json, 22 entries). File as a NEW finding of a pre-existing defect: not a regression, not a carryover stub. What is new this cycle is the §4.1 guard, which converts the leak from 'dust escapes' into 'the pot can only escape this way'.

original.type: regression of a fixed mainnet incident / incentive-mechanism nullification
original.description: Duplicate `rewardTokens` entries do not 'fail closed'. Each duplicate snapshots the same pre-loop balance B (L434) and the payout pass transfers B once per entry with no cumulative cap, succeeding while k*B <= B + D where D is this batch's own mid-loop donation. §4.5 and the NatSpec at L258-L266 assert the opposite and use that assertion as the stated justification for having no dedupe pass. Confirming the profiler's LOCAL-BM20-001 and adding the mainnet magnitude: this restores, bit for bit, the live incident that story-016's snapshot-before-loop was deployed to fix.
original.incidentLineage: phoenix-phase-2-staging/docs/BatchNFTMint/self-refund-fix-and-migration-plan.md documents the live bug (tx 0x6d71d6fd…, block 25242986): a 40-batcher's own 51.77 USDC donation was refunded to them and 'Pot left for the next minter: 0'. The operational bleed-stop zeroed batchDonationSize on the index-4 pooler; MigrateBatchNFTMinter.s.sol:342/:489-493 RESTORES it to 15 in-broadcast after migration. Story-016 (5f863d2) fixed it in code by snapshotting before the loop. Story-022's no-dedupe policy re-opens it under caller control.

quantification.atObservedShape: count=40, 15% donation, price 12.94 USDS: D = 77.64 USDC vs observed pot B = 88.07 USDC. D < B, so k=2 reverts — the §4.5 claim HOLDS here. This is the mechanism's best case and it is narrow.
quantification.attackerControlsCount: `count` is caller-chosen and unbounded above nudgeSize=40, and D scales linearly with it while B does not. At count=400: D = 776.40 USDC, k = floor(1 + D/B) = 9, payout = 9*B = 792.59 USDC of which 704.53 USDC (90.7% of D) is the batcher's own donation clawed back. Residual left for the next claimant: 71.87 USDC.
quantification.steadyState: Back-to-back batching drives B to exactly the previous batch's donation, so D >= B holds by construction (prices ramp at 1 bps/mint) and k=2 always succeeds. PoC: prior pot 77.64 -> paid out 155.28 -> 0.00 left behind. The donate-forward mechanic is nullified permanently, not occasionally.

original.attackScenario:
1. Batcher observes pot B on the BalancerPooler batch minter.
2. Picks count >= 40 (larger count => larger own donation D).
3. Calls batchMint(count, self, cost, [USDC, USDC, ... k times], [0,...,0]) with k = floor(1 + D/B).
4. Snapshot writes B into all k slots; payout transfers B k times, succeeding because the mint loop has meanwhile deposited D.
5. Batcher receives B + (k-1)*B ~= B + D: the prior pot AND their own 15% donation.
original.economicImpact: Converts every batch mint into a 15%-discounted mint at protocol expense. The 15% is not the batcher's money in any meaningful sense — BalancerPoolerV2.sol:212-213 carves it out of the mint payment BEFORE pooling (`poolingUSDS = amount - donationUSDS`), so recapturing it diverts value that would otherwise have backed the NFT or seeded the pot. Correcting the profiler's framing: this is NOT purely self-funded. Secondary impact: the next claimant's seed can be driven to exactly zero, and §4.2's load-bearing documented invariant is false (Law-2 faithfulness break against docs/multi-token-nudge.md §4.2/§4.5).
original.profitability: Not profitable in isolation (the batcher still pays 85% of the mint cost), but strictly dominant over the honest call for any batcher who is minting anyway, and it gives a front-running searcher a ~15% cost advantage in the winner-take-all pot auction over any honest claimer — see ECON-003.
affectedParties: the next claimant, whose seed is destroyed
original.testCoverageGap: test/BatchNFTMinterMultiTokenNudge.t.sol:656 test_DuplicateRewardTokenFailsClosed never calls setPerMintDonation, so it runs with D == 0 — the one configuration §4.2 explicitly says does not occur in production. The witness test certifies the property under an assumption the spec denies.
original.recommendation: Cap cumulative payout per token against the live balance in _payRewards: `amount = Math.min(snapshot[i], IERC20(t).balanceOf(address(this)) - paidThisPass)` is O(n) and preserves the no-dedupe stance. Equivalently, assert the post-payout balance is >= preLoopBalance - totalSnapshotted. Then rewrite §4.5 and re-run the witness test WITH donations configured.

original.type: MEV / incentive misalignment on the new caller-selected path
original.description: The old M-01 (MEV nudge-pot front-run) is recorded 'fixed', but the fix was the minReward slippage floor, which §5 is explicit only protects the LOSER from paying mint costs for a sniped pot — it does nothing to prevent the front-run. Story-022 does not introduce a new front-run primitive, but it changes the auction's economics in two ways worth recording rather than closing.
detail: (a) Cost asymmetry from ECON-002. A searcher who duplicates entries qualifies at ~85% of the honest cost, so in any gas/priority auction for the pot the duplicating searcher can outbid every honest claimer by up to D. The winner of the pot is now systematically the participant exploiting the §4.5 gap.

(b) `recipient` is caller-chosen and need not be msg.sender (L303 only checks non-zero), and both the NFTs and the entire reward payout go to `recipient` while the payment-token sweep goes to msg.sender. A searcher can therefore split the legs across addresses, which frustrates attribution but confers no additional extraction. Not a finding on its own.

(c) L-05 (minReward==0 opts out of the guard, wont-fix) is load-bearing here: a UI that defaults minRewards to zeros leaves every honest caller fully exposed to the snipe, and story-022 multiplied the number of zeros a UI must populate from one scalar to an array.
original.economicImpact: No direct loss beyond ECON-002. The documented MEV posture (§5 'bot competition here is a subsidy to the protocol') stays true only while premise (1) holds; see ECON-004.
original.recommendation: No separate code change; fixing ECON-002 restores auction symmetry. Consider a UI-level requirement that minRewards be populated non-zero.

original.function: §1 'Why the honeypot framing does not apply'
original.description: §1 claims 'by construction it is a fraction of the cost of the nudgeSize mints required to qualify' and 'there is no configuration of this mechanism under which claiming is profitable-in-isolation'. Neither is established by construction. See watch19PremiseReDerivation above: (1) the PRIMARY funder is StableYieldAccumulator's 20-30% nudgeSplit drip (StableYieldAccumulator.sol:512-516), an unbounded time-accumulating stream with no relationship to mint cost — nothing in BatchNFTMinter bounds the pot, only MEV competition does; (2) minted units are freely transferable ERC1155 and unlock 30%/45% phUSD staking APY, so the claimant's true cost is mintCost minus the NFT's yield NPV, strictly below what §1 assumes. The 'over-funding is the sender's error' disclaimer at L56-L61 does not cover this: the drip IS the designed funding path (DeployBatchNFTMinter.s.sol:31-33 names it 'PRIMARY 30% drip'), not an erroneous over-fund.
original.economicImpact: No standalone loss — the observed margin is ~6x (88 USDC pot vs ~518 USDS for 40 mints). This is the amplifier that sets how bad ECON-001 and ECON-002 can get, and it removes the safety argument the design leans on. It also means a prolonged period of no batching (bots offline, gas spike, UI outage) lets the pot cross the profitability line with no on-chain brake.
original.profitability: A claim becomes profitable-in-isolation once pot > nudgeSize*mintPrice - NFT_NPV. Nothing enforces the inequality.
original.recommendation: Either (a) cap the claimable payout per batch as a function of the payment actually routed through the batch (which would restore the 'by construction' claim honestly), or (b) rewrite §1 to state that the bound is empirical and maintained by bot competition plus operator discipline on nudgeSplit, and record the NFT's yield value in the break-even. Do not leave the stronger claim standing.
original.law1Note: Surfaced under WATCH-19-nudge-law1-reopen-trigger. Premise (2) has stopped holding outright; premise (1) survives on evidence, not construction. Neither is inherited as 'already known'.

original.description: Two reporting defects that mislead off-chain consumers on exactly the paths where value moved unexpectedly. (a) `totalPaid = paymentAmount > remaining ? paymentAmount - remaining : 0` floors at 0, so whenever the contract held a pre-existing payment-token balance the return value reports 0 net spend while the caller is net POSITIVE — this is the reporting face of ECON-001 and reads as 'free batch' rather than 'you took the pot'. (b) NudgePaid(recipient, token, amount) at L459 emits the SNAPSHOT amount, not the delivered amount, so on any fee-on-transfer or negatively-rebasing reward token the event over-reports what the recipient received.
original.economicImpact: No direct loss. Any indexer, accounting job, or UI keyed on totalPaid or NudgePaid inherits the error.
original.recommendation: Fixing ECON-001's sweep bound fixes (a) as a side effect. For (b), either emit the balance-delta or rename the field to make the snapshot semantics explicit.

original.description: §4.4 explicitly brings fee-on-transfer into scope by documenting the decision not to defend against it: minRewards[i] floors the contract's PRE-TRANSFER balance (L431), never the delivered amount, so a FoT or negatively-rebasing token clears the floor and under-delivers. The profiler's residue is that the shortfall lands on `recipient`, an arbitrary caller-chosen address that never consented to the tradeoff the NatSpec frames as 'at the caller's discretion'.
original.verdict: STAYS QA — it does not rise to Medium, and the fact that §4.4 documents it does not rescue it. The reasoning: the caller chooses BOTH the reward token AND the recipient. There is no path by which party A's choice of a taxed token imposes a loss on an unrelated party B — the only exposure is an integrator harming its own users through its own recipient parameter, which is an integration-quality issue, not a protocol vulnerability. The fee accrues to the token's own fee sink, never to the caller, so there is no extraction. This lands on the C4 known-invalid side (weird-ERC20 / user input) even with §4.4 bringing it into scope: documenting a risk makes it in-scope for DISCUSSION, it does not manufacture an attack path that the value flow does not support.
original.economicImpact: Bounded by the tax rate on an asset the protocol does not use; borne by a recipient the caller selected.
affectedParties: a third-party recipient of an integrator's batch
original.recommendation: No code change (agreeing with §4.4). Reword the NatSpec at L252-L256 so the risk is attributed to `recipient` rather than to 'the caller', so an integrator reading it understands who actually eats the shortfall.

original.description: A migration necessarily drains the pool to zero (finalizeAndReset requires totalStaked == 0) and then refills it one operator-chosen slice at a time. Emissions resume the instant slice 1 lands, but slice-N users are still parked in the migrator's custody and earn nothing. Because the budget is shared, the emissions slice-1 users collect during the staggered re-injection are drawn from the same rewardBudget that funds every later user's runway. Time-in-pool - and therefore payout - is decided entirely by which migrateIn slice the operator puts a user in, a variable no user controls and no user can observe in advance.
original.codeSnippet:
// InPlaceNFTStakerMigrator.migrateIn(start, end) -> staker.depositFor(user, amt)
// NFTStakerPriceScaledMigrateReady.depositFor L901: _recomputeSchedule();  // emissions resume for whoever is already in
original.economicImpact: Value transfer between users, bounded by targetAPY * (gap between first and last slice) * slice-1 notional. Protocol solvency is unaffected (asserted in PoC).
original.attackScenario:
1. Alice and Bob hold identical 10-unit positions, parked at the same instant by one migrateOut.
2. Operator runs finalizeAndReset, then migrateIn(0,1) -> Alice back in.
3. Three days of operational lag (rewire, multisig, gas window).
4. migrateIn(0,1) -> Bob back in.
5. Both sit staked a further 30 days and claim.
PoC test_ECON_A_migrateInOrderingIsAValueTransfer: Alice 40.685 phUSD vs Bob 36.986 phUSD - a 1000 bps (10.00%) gap over identical wall-clock exposure, exactly targetAPY(45%) * 3 days * 1000 phUSD notional = 3.699 phUSD.
original.profitability: Not an attacker-profit vector; it is an operator-ordering footgun (Law 3: a competent non-malicious owner would be surprised that slice order decides payout). At MAX_TARGET_APY (50%) and a 7-day staggered migration the transfer reaches ~0.96% of the migrated notional.
original.affectedParties: Users placed in later migrateIn slices (and, cross-staker, later migrate() batches).
original.worseOnSibling: The same class is worse on src/NFTStakerDepletion.sol, where rate = budget/windowSeconds is independent of totalStaked, so slice-1 users split the ENTIRE pool-wide emission stream among themselves. PoC test_ECON_G_depletionMigrateInOrderingOverPaysSliceOne: slice-1 user earns 120% of the slice-2 user (48.98 vs 40.76 phUSD) vs 110% on the price-scaled copy. This is the migration-path reachability of the phlimbo-ea Linear-Depletion / run-18 M-01 rate-drift class; story-020's fix addressed the unstake path, not this one.
original.recommendation: Set targetAPY to 0 immediately after finalizeAndReset and restore it only after the final migrateIn slice lands - emissions are then zero for the whole staggered window and slice order carries no economic weight. (Alternatively re-inject in a single transaction; ECON-04 shows gas permits ~400 users per block.) Document whichever is chosen as a mandatory runbook step.
original.possiblyIntentional: Partially - 'you are not staked, you do not earn' is defensible. What makes it reportable is that the operator, not the user, chose the un-staked interval, via a migrate-on-behalf primitive.

original.type: cross-contract griefing / state-machine livelock + silent zero-yield stake
original.description: This is the cross-contract escalation of profile LOCAL-001, and it changes that finding's character from 'a griefer could' to 'an ordinary impatient user will, using the migrator's own documented escape hatch'. claimTimedOut hands the ERC1155 back to a parked user while the staker is still Migrating. stake() carries no poolState gate, so the user can immediately re-stake. That makes totalStaked > 0, which permanently blocks finalizeAndReset - the ONLY transition back to Active - which in turn blocks depositFor and therefore migrateIn for EVERY other parked user. Evicting the re-staker via batchMigrate re-parks their stake and RESTARTS their migrationTimeout clock, so the loop can repeat. Separately, the re-staker earns exactly zero for as long as the pool stays frozen: accRewardPerShare is pinned, so the contract silently accepts a stake it will never pay on.
original.economicImpact: Migration availability: the in-place rewire cannot complete. Plus a silent per-user yield loss for anyone who re-stakes into a frozen pool.
original.attackScenario:
1. Operator initiateMigration + migrateOut(alice, bob). The rewire runs long (migrationTimeout floor is only MIN_TIMEOUT = 1 day).
2. Alice claimTimedOut -> receives her 10 units back.
3. Alice re-stakes 10 units. Succeeds: totalStaked = 10.
4. Ten days pass; pendingReward(alice) == 0 (asserted).
5. finalizeAndReset reverts 'NFTStaker: stake outstanding'; migrateIn(0,1) for Bob reverts 'NFTStaker: not active'.
6. Operator migrateOut(alice) to evict - claimableAt(alice) is reset to now + TIMEOUT, re-arming the loop.
PoC test_ECON_B_timeoutHatchRestakeLivelocksFinalizeAndReset (all six steps asserted).
original.profitability: Zero attacker profit (the re-staker earns nothing). Pure cost griefing, or - more likely - accidental, since the hatch and the stake button are both legitimate documented user actions.
original.affectedParties: All other parked users (re-injection blocked); the re-staker (silent zero yield).
original.recommendation: Primary: pause() for the whole migration - stake is whenNotPaused while every migration primitive and every user escape is deliberately callable while paused, so this closes the vector completely and traps nobody. Make it a mandatory runbook step. Structural alternative: add require(poolState == PoolState.Active) to stake(), which also removes the silent zero-yield surprise.
original.possiblyIntentional: The freeze semantics are intentional; the unguarded stake() during Migrating appears to be an oversight inherited from the depletion copy (its ledgered L-03).

original.type: MEV / informational edge across the migration seam
original.description: userMigrate is permissionless by design (the frozen-state escape hatch). A user who is watching can self-exit the frozen source staker and immediately stake into the Active target staker themselves, jumping the operator's batch queue and capturing the APY that ECON-01 denies to users who wait for their batch. Same root economic cause as ECON-01 (unequal time-in-pool during a migration funded from a shared budget) but a distinct actor and a distinct mechanism, so it is filed separately: mitigating ECON-01 by re-ordering slices does not touch this, and mitigating this by removing userMigrate would break the escape hatch.
original.economicImpact: Sophisticated users systematically out-earn passive users across every migration, out of the shared reward budget.
original.attackScenario:
1. Operator initiateMigration on the source (cross-staker or cross-model).
2. Alice front-runs the operator: userMigrate() -> stake() on the target.
3. Operator's batch for Bob lands 5 days later.
4. Both sit 30 further days and claim.
PoC test_ECON_H_selfAdvanceBeatsOperatorBatchOrder: Alice 43.151 phUSD vs Bob 36.986 phUSD - a 1666 bps (16.66%) edge.
original.profitability: Profitable for any user with a watcher; cost is two transactions. Requires the target staker to be Active and to share stakedToken/stakedId (which the migrator's own wiring requires anyway).
original.recommendation: The ECON-01 remedy (targetAPY = 0 across the migration window) neutralises this too. Otherwise disclose the self-advance option to all users so the edge is not informational.

dispositions.reason: REFUTED WITH MEASUREMENT — quantified refutation of profile LOCAL-006's DoS-ceiling warning. Measured at N=40 users with a live mock dispatcher hook and non-zero pendingMint: price-scaled 70,312 gas/user (2,812,503 total) vs depletion 55,565 gas/user — a 1.27x premium, not an order of magnitude. 30M block / 70,312 = 426 users per transaction. The real BalancerPoolerMintDebtHook.pull() is a no-op after the first loop iteration (mintDebt is zeroed on the first pull), so the mock is representative. No realistic DoS ceiling; no code change needed. Runbook note only: size migrateIn slices at <= 100 users — a comfortable margin, not a constraint.
